title: What is self-compassion?
citation: Neff, K. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and identity, 2(2), 85-101.
content:
What is self-compassion?

Self-compassion means responding to yourself with the same understanding, care and encouragement that you would naturally offer someone you care about. It does not mean ignoring mistakes or pretending everything is fine. Instead, it means recognising that everyone struggles, treating yourself kindly when things are difficult and responding in a way that supports growth rather than shame. Research suggests that self-compassion is linked to greater emotional wellbeing, resilience and healthier ways of coping with setbacks.

Isn't self-compassion just letting myself off the hook?

Many people worry that being kind to themselves will make them lazy, unmotivated, or less accountable. In reality, self-compassion is not about avoiding responsibility. It means acknowledging mistakes honestly while responding in a constructive way, rather than attacking yourself. People who practise self-compassion are often more willing to learn from setbacks because they spend less energy on self-blame and more energy on making meaningful changes.

Why is my inner voice so much harsher than I'd be with a friend?

Our inner critic often develops as a way of trying to protect us from failure, rejection, or disappointment. Early experiences, high expectations, perfectionism, or repeated criticism can teach the brain that being hard on ourselves is the best way to stay motivated or avoid mistakes. Although this strategy may have developed with good intentions, harsh self-criticism usually increases stress, shame and anxiety rather than helping us perform better.

What does self-compassion actually look like?

Self-compassion is not about telling yourself that everything is perfect. Instead, it sounds balanced, supportive and realistic. Rather than saying, "I'm useless because I made a mistake," a self-compassionate response might be, "That was difficult and I didn't handle it the way I hoped. Everyone makes mistakes and I can learn from this." The goal is not to lower your standards, but to speak to yourself in a way that helps you move forward instead of keeping you stuck.

Self-compassion vs self-esteem: what's the difference?

Self-esteem is often based on how positively we evaluate ourselves, sometimes comparing ourselves with others or judging our achievements. Self-compassion works differently. It is not about believing you are better than others or feeling confident all the time. Instead, it is about treating yourself with kindness regardless of whether you succeed or fail. This makes self-compassion more stable because it does not depend on constant achievement or external validation.

Why do I criticise myself even when nothing went wrong?

For some people, self-criticism becomes such a familiar habit that it continues even when there is no obvious reason for it. The brain may automatically scan for flaws or assume that self-criticism is necessary to stay motivated or avoid future mistakes. Over time, this habit can become the default way of responding to yourself. Recognising this pattern is an important first step, because habits of self-criticism can be replaced with more balanced and compassionate ways of thinking.

How do I practise self-compassion?

Self-compassion develops through repeated practice rather than happening overnight. A helpful starting point is to pause when you notice self-critical thoughts and ask yourself how you would respond if a close friend were in the same situation. You can also acknowledge that difficult emotions are part of being human, remind yourself that imperfection is something everyone experiences and choose words that are supportive rather than attacking. Like any new skill, self-compassion becomes more natural with consistent practice.
